Feldstein gives a spirited, highly enjoyable performance, and her freshness drew squeals of appreciation from what seemed like a large contingent of very vocal young female fans on a recent press night. But she never quite makes the material soar, and this is a rickety vehicle that needs a supernova to put gas in its tank.
She radiates the hunger, wry humor and fragility to be an unlikely heroine for a new generation.
Feldstein can only do so much as a Broadway star with what she has to offer at this point.
The fact that this amiable young performer does battle with a most fearsome ghost and survives with her dignity and our collective sense of relief intact should not be underappreciated.
Feldstein's Fanny is more sweet than sassy, more earnest than manic, which makes for a perfectly pleasant performance that doesn't quite capture the character's supposed star quality.
But this is a musical, one with some full-tilt belting, and her singing just isn’t up to par.
But you know a production of Funny Girl hasn't clicked when you leave thinking, Well, at least it was pretty.
It seems brutal to place a woman in such an exposed position, where a whole Broadway production rests on notes she can’t sustain.
Rather than incandescent, though, Feldstein’s star turn is an earthbound affair, best when she’s executing the comedy aspect of musical comedy, and less compelling at the music part.
And without a stupendous Fanny to thrill and distract, the musical’s manifold faults become painfully evident.
What a 2022 audience may find exasperating is the unresolved dichotomy of its leading character.
But on the stage of the Theatre, one feels a hollowness—a well-rehearsed and dutiful hollowness—where there should be restless combustion.
Watching Feldstein trying to get to grips with the larger-than-life personality of the vaudeville legend Fanny Brice is a distinctly uncomfortable experience.
This sorely lacking new production rains on the old musical’s parade.
Every so often if you are very lucky, you see a performance you'll be talking about for years.
Funny Girl is a brilliant work, and with Feldstein, radiates pure theatrical joy.
Michele stands alone as a singular Broadway performer, one who can pack a house and command a crowd.

But perhaps knowing that Funny Girl is capable of being middling with a few precious high points could finally lift the veil of mythology from this untouchable property.

Sometimes it is time to call a bluff. I'm calling it.

The totality of her performance is a fascinating instance of delusional adequacy.
It’s a witless cliché, and a counterproductive one.

With Isobel Lennart's book reworked some by Harvey Fierstein, Funny Girl is at its best when the comedy is front and center, and Feldstein is a first-rate comedian who knows how to mine a scene for every laugh.
Feldstein tries, and comes nowhere close to succeeding, but reveals something deeper: take Barbra away, and Funny Girl is not a good musical.
I have no doubt that Funny Girl will experience a lengthy extended run—to return again to see either Michele or her understudy, Julie Benko, would truly be a treat.
Future discussions of this Funny Girl will be unable to ignore the elephant in the room: would its fate have been seriously altered by a different casting decision?

tn.cat: Best Featured Actor in a Musical

cn.t: Critics are sharply divided on this revival, with Beanie Feldstein's casting as a major sticking point—many find her vocally miscast. Lea Michele's later takeover earns considerably warmer reviews, with praise for her commanding performance.

sg.ra: August Wilson has no traditional proscenium arch and a 38-ft-wide stage opening that ends at the side walls, so mid-center orchestra rows D-G pick up the full width no other Broadway house exposes; the lower stage (which extends over the usual pit area) also means you are not losing actors' feet here the way you would in a standard proscenium house. Rows E-G sit ahead of the mezzanine overhang line (row L) so nothing is cropped overhead.

August Wilson's mezzanine is the house's only elevated level (no balcony above it), so front-mezz row A looks straight down onto the low, pit-extended stage with nothing overhead - an unusually clean overhead angle you cannot get in the three-tier houses across 52nd. Row A is also the one mezz row noted for better legroom in this otherwise tight-rowed house, and it sits well forward of the overhang start at row L.

Because August Wilson is a single-balcony house, the mezzanine keeps an effective rake all the way back and is not shadowed by an upper level the way multi-tier Shubert houses are. Mid-center rows D-H stay ahead of where the overhang would cut the top of the stage (the overhang affects the orchestra below from row L onward, not the mezz itself), and row H is specifically cited for extra legroom plus elevation over the row in front - unusual in this tight-legroom house. Forum consensus on BWW and TripAdvisor repeatedly recommends mezz over mid/rear orchestra at the same price.

August Wilson's front sides are flanked by Roman arches and decorative columns (a feature unique to this 1925 Crane/Franzheim house) - they don't block views but they physically frame side orchestra wings, and the 38-ft-wide proscenium-less opening means side seats can still see stage-width action the way they can't in narrower houses. Front-row sides (A-C) feel uncomfortably close; mid-side D-G is the workable band.

The August Wilson mezzanine overhang begins at row L and by rows V-ZZ it cuts off the top of the stage - a specific cutoff repeatedly confirmed by SeatPlan, Headout, and the Tripadvisor forum Q&A about row P. Because this is a single-balcony house the overhang is deep and low, and a BWW forum poster who sat Orch row W for Jersey Boys confirmed losing overhead projections. For the same price, front-to-mid mezzanine always wins here.

August Wilson's mezz tops out at row Q (it skips row I) and there is no balcony above it, so rear mezz is physically the back wall of the house. SeatPlan calls rear mezz up to row M 'impressively good' value, but beyond M you're at the back wall of a 1,239-seat house with no upper level to compare against; sightlines remain unobstructed thanks to the effective rake but binoculars help for intimate dramas. Tight legroom here since row H's legroom bump does not apply this far back.
